summary: An older (typical) antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia. It can work well, but has real risks, especially movement side effects, tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements, often of the face or mouth, that can last), sleepiness, and a boxed warning about a higher risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis.
description: Perphenazine is a typical antipsychotic that can reduce hallucinations, delusions, paranoia and severe agitation by blocking dopamine signals in the brain. It can also cause movement side effects (restlessness, stiffness, tremor), sleepiness, dizziness, and dizziness or feeling faint when standing up (a drop in blood pressure). Long-term use can lead to tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements that may be permanent). In older adults with dementia-related psychosis, antipsychotics raise the risk of death; perphenazine is not approved for that use.
patient_summary: Perphenazine can help with schizophrenia symptoms like hallucinations, delusions, and severe agitation, but it can also make you feel slowed down, stiff, or restless. Movement side effects are the big watch-out. Long-term use can cause tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements that can become permanent). It also carries a boxed warning: in older adults with dementia-related psychosis, antipsychotics raise the risk of death—this medication isn’t approved for that.

primary.context: Labeled for schizophrenia. Often reserved for situations where a first-generation antipsychotic makes sense based on prior response, patient preference, access, or side effect tradeoffs.

off_label.context: May be used in select cases of severe agitation related to psychosis, but dosing and setting should be guided by a psychiatry specialist and local protocols.

therapeutic_response.display: Schizophrenia: early effects may be noticed within 1 to 2 weeks; fuller benefit often builds over 4 to 6 weeks

common_adverse_effects.effect: Stiffness, shaking or restlessness (movement side effects)
common_adverse_effects.notes: This is the signature risk zone for perphenazine. Watch for restlessness (akathisia), stiffness, tremor, slowed movement, or jaw/neck muscle tightness. These can show up early and can get worse with dose increases.
Some people feel calmer but sleepy or slowed down—especially early in treatment. If you’re too sedated to function, that’s a dosing/timing problem worth fixing, not a life sentence.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dizziness when standing up (drop in blood pressure)
common_adverse_effects.notes: Feeling lightheaded when you stand up can happen, especially while the dose is being raised. This matters because it raises the risk of falls, especially in older adults.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, trouble peeing
common_adverse_effects.notes: Perphenazine causes these less than some similar medicines, but they can still happen, especially if combined with other medicines that have the same drying effects.

Possible period changes, breast tenderness or enlargement, milky discharge from the nipples, changes in sex drive, and erection or ejaculation problems. If these show up, prolactin can be checked and the plan adjusted.

serious_risks.risk: Tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements of the face, tongue, jaw or limbs) that can become permanent
A rare emergency (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS): fever, severe stiffness, confusion, unstable blood pressure or heart rate. This is a medical emergency.
Serious arrhythmias: Palpitations, fainting, sudden collapse — EMERGENCY
Severe blood problems (for example, agranulocytosis, a dangerous drop in white blood cells): infections, fever, sore throat. Get checked urgently.
Jaundice or liver injury: Yellow skin/eyes, dark urine, severe fatigue
Seizures: Especially in people with seizure history or other risk factors
Aspiration pneumonia risk: Swallowing problems, choking episodes, cough/fever—especially in older adults

safety.black_box_warning: Older adults with dementia-related psychosis who take antipsychotic medicines have a higher risk of death. In studies that compared antipsychotics with placebo (usually lasting about 10 weeks), the death rate was about 4.5% with antipsychotics vs about 2.6% with placebo (roughly 1.6–1.7 times higher). Deaths were often from heart problems (for example, heart failure, sudden death) or infections (for example, pneumonia). Perphenazine is not approved to treat dementia-related psychosis.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to perphenazine or any component of the formulation
Severely slowed brain function (coma, or taking large doses of other medicines that slow the brain)
Subcortical brain damage with or without hypothalamic damage (known or suspected)

precautions: Tardive dyskinesia (TD): Involuntary movements that can become irreversible; risk increases with dose and duration, and is higher in older adults (especially older women)
Movement side effects: akathisia (a strong inner restlessness), muscle spasms, Parkinson-like stiffness and slowness, and tremor; these can be severe and appear early
A rare but life-threatening reaction (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS): fever, stiffness, confusion, and swings in heart rate, blood pressure or sweating
Cardiac conduction changes and serious arrhythmias have been reported with phenothiazines—even at therapeutic doses
Dizziness or feeling faint when standing up (a drop in blood pressure) and falls, especially in older adults or while the dose is being raised

Blood problems: drops in white blood cells (leukopenia), including the infection-fighting type (neutropenia), and agranulocytosis (a dangerous near-total loss); the medicine is stopped if severe changes develop
Aspiration risk: Antipsychotics can be linked to esophageal dysmotility and aspiration pneumonia (risk increases with age)
Seizure threshold: First-generation antipsychotics can lower seizure threshold
Depression and suicidality: Use caution; limit quantities if suicide risk is a concern
Liver risk: should not be used if you have liver damage; watch for yellowing skin or eyes (jaundice) or abnormal liver tests

interactions.interactant: Alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, sedating sleep meds, sedating antihistamines
interactions.mechanism: Additive CNS depression: more sedation, impaired coordination, falls, and in severe cases breathing suppression (especially when multiple sedatives are combined).
interactions.action: Avoid mixing when possible. If combination is clinically necessary, use lowest effective doses and monitor closely—especially early on.

interactions.mechanism: Higher risk of dangerous rhythm problems when multiple QT-risk agents are combined, especially with electrolyte abnormalities.
interactions.action: Review the full med list for QT risk. Correct low potassium/magnesium and consider ECG monitoring when risk is elevated.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that slow how your body breaks down perphenazine (CYP2D6 inhibitors), or having a body that naturally breaks it down slowly
interactions.mechanism: More perphenazine in your body can increase movement side effects, sleepiness and other side effects.
interactions.action: Use caution. A lower dose and closer checks may be needed if you take one of these medicines or naturally break it down slowly.

interactions.mechanism: Additive blood pressure lowering may worsen dizziness and falls.
interactions.action: Your blood pressure may be checked sitting and standing, and treatment adjusted if you have symptoms.

interactions.interactant: Medicines with drying effects such as dry mouth and constipation (anticholinergics)
interactions.mechanism: More constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion (especially in older adults).
interactions.action: Avoid piling up several medicines with these effects, and watch for bowel and bladder problems.

interactions.interactant: Dopamine agonists (eg, medications used for Parkinson symptoms)
interactions.mechanism: Pharmacologic “tug-of-war”: perphenazine blocks dopamine, which can reduce the effect of dopamine-boosting meds and worsen parkinsonism.
interactions.action: Use caution and coordinate with neurology/psychiatry when both are needed.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Mental status and function: symptom change, agitation, suicidality, and overall functioning at every visit
Movement side effects: checked at every visit, again about 4 weeks after starting and after dose changes, with a formal rating scale at least once a year (or every 6 months if you are at high risk)
Tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements that can last): watched for at every visit, with formal screening at least once a year (or more often if you are at high risk)
Vital signs and blood pressure sitting and standing: especially when starting or raising the dose and in older adults; fall risk checked as needed
Weight/BMI: every visit for the first 6 months, then at least quarterly; consider waist circumference at baseline and annually
Metabolic labs: fasting glucose/HbA1c and lipid panel about 4 months after initiation and then at least annually (more often if abnormal)
Blood salts and sodium: especially in older adults (risk of low blood sodium, which can cause confusion, headache or seizures) and when needed
Blood count (CBC): when needed, and more closely if your white blood cell count has been low or a medicine has lowered it before; the medicine is stopped if a severe blood problem develops
Liver function tests: as clinically indicated; discontinue if abnormalities occur; be alert for jaundice symptoms
Cardiac risk: consider ECG and electrolyte review when baseline risk is elevated or when combining with QT-risk meds
Adherence and safety behaviors: check at every visit; review sedation, driving safety, and substance use

special_populations.pregnancy: Class-level data for first-generation antipsychotics do not show a clear large increase in major congenital malformations, but individual-agent data are limited. Antipsychotic use in the third trimester can increase the risk of newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, abnormal tone, tremor, sleepiness, feeding problems, respiratory distress). Treatment decisions should use shared decision-making: relapse prevention matters, and stopping an effective medication can be risky. Use the lowest effective dose of a single agent when possible and avoid polytherapy unless clearly needed.
special_populations.lactation: Perphenazine passes into breast milk. Limited data from one reported case suggest the baby gets a low dose, and that baby had no side effects. However, babies exposed to antipsychotics through breast milk can become sleepy or irritable, feed poorly, or have movement problems. If you breastfeed while taking perphenazine, watch your baby closely, especially if the baby was premature or small at birth, or if you take other sedating medicines.
special_populations.geriatric: A high-risk medicine for older adults. Antipsychotics may be unsuitable for behavior changes in dementia or sudden confusion (delirium) unless non-medicine approaches have failed and there is a risk of harm. Boxed warning: higher risk of death in dementia-related psychosis. Older adults are also more vulnerable to dizziness when standing up (a drop in blood pressure), falls, sleepiness, choking or inhaling food or drink, low blood sodium, and movement side effects. Treatment starts low, is raised slowly step by step, and is reviewed often.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Use with caution. Monitor renal function clinically; discontinue if concerning abnormalities occur.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Should not be used if you have liver damage. Liver function is checked during treatment, and the medicine is stopped if important changes appear.

pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Perphenazine: 1 to 3 hours; active metabolite: 2 to 4 hours
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Perphenazine: 9 to 12 hours; active metabolite: 10 to 19 hours
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism; CYP2D6 is a major pathway (genetic differences can matter)

dosing.titration: Perphenazine dosing for schizophrenia is usually divided across the day. Many people do best when the dose is increased slowly and kept at the lowest effective maintenance dose to reduce EPS and other side effects. First-episode psychosis often requires lower starting doses because sensitivity to adverse effects tends to be higher.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: If perphenazine is being stopped (and it’s not an emergency safety situation), a gradual taper is usually the move—especially in chronic psychotic disorders. The goal is to reduce withdrawal symptoms and catch early relapse signs before they become a full crisis.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Perphenazine is a first-generation (typical) antipsychotic primarily used to treat schizophrenia. In psychiatry, it’s mainly about reducing psychosis symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, paranoia) and helping stabilize behavior when symptoms are severe.
items: {link:condition:schizophrenia:Schizophrenia}: Helps reduce hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, and disorganized thinking
Severe psychosis-related agitation: Sometimes used when psychosis is driving dangerous agitation (specialist-guided)

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: The voices got less intense. Like they were farther away.
My paranoia eased up enough that I could actually leave the house.
My thoughts stopped spiraling so hard.
I felt calmer, but also kind of heavy and slowed down.
It helped me sleep, but mornings were rough at first.
My brain felt quieter… and my body felt sleepy.
items.note: Sedation can show up early, especially during dose increases.

quotes: I couldn’t sit still. It was like my legs needed to run.
My body felt stiff and tight, like I was moving through mud.
My hands had a slight tremor I didn’t have before.
items.note: Movement side effects are a bigger deal with typical antipsychotics. If this happens, it’s not something to “power through”—tell your prescriber.

quotes: I felt less distressed… but also less emotionally reactive.
It quieted the chaos, but I felt a bit blank.
I wasn’t as scared, but I also wasn’t as excited about anything.

sections.intro: Perphenazine can be helpful, but the “feel” can be a mix of calmer brain + annoying body side effects. Here’s the vibe people commonly describe:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Perphenazine isn’t a “take it and instantly feel normal” medication. With schizophrenia, improvement usually builds over weeks.
key_points: Hours: Blood levels rise after a dose, but symptom improvement usually doesn’t track hour-to-hour
1 to 2 weeks: Early changes may show up (less agitation, less intensity of hallucinations/delusions)
4 to 6 weeks: Bigger improvements often become clearer with consistent dosing
1 to 3 hours: Time to peak level after a dose (perphenazine)
9 to 12 hours: Typical half-life for the parent drug

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Perphenazine can be effective for schizophrenia symptoms, especially positive symptoms like hallucinations and delusions. The main clinical tradeoff is tolerability: compared with many second-generation antipsychotics, perphenazine can carry a higher risk of extrapyramidal symptoms (restlessness, stiffness, tremor) and tardive dyskinesia over time.
sections.clinical_details: In real-world practice, response depends on dose, sensitivity to side effects, prior antipsychotic exposure, and whether movement symptoms are proactively monitored and treated. Many people who do well on perphenazine do best on the lowest effective maintenance dose.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: BOXED WARNING: Increased risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis. Perphenazine is not approved for that use.
sections.black_box: Older adults with dementia-related psychosis who take antipsychotic medicines have a higher risk of death. In studies that compared antipsychotics with placebo (usually lasting about 10 weeks), the death rate was about 4.5% with antipsychotics vs about 2.6% with placebo (roughly 1.6–1.7 times higher). Deaths were often from heart problems (for example, heart failure, sudden death) or infections (for example, pneumonia). Perphenazine is not approved to treat dementia-related psychosis.
other: Tardive dyskinesia (TD): Involuntary movements that can become irreversible; risk increases with dose and duration, and is higher in older adults (especially older women)
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS): Akathisia, dystonia, parkinsonism, tremor—can be severe and appear early
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): Rare but life-threatening (fever, rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability)
Cardiac conduction changes and serious arrhythmias have been reported with phenothiazines—even at therapeutic doses
Orthostatic hypotension and falls: Especially in older adults or during titration
Blood dyscrasias: Leukopenia, neutropenia, agranulocytosis; stop if severe abnormalities develop
Aspiration risk: Antipsychotics can be linked to esophageal dysmotility and aspiration pneumonia (risk increases with age)
Seizure threshold: First-generation antipsychotics can lower seizure threshold
Depression and suicidality: Use caution; limit quantities if suicide risk is a concern
Hepatic risk: Contraindicated in liver damage; monitor for jaundice or abnormal liver tests
patient_counseling: If you’re over 65 and this is being considered for dementia-related behaviors: pause. This class carries a real increased risk of death in that setting.
If you develop severe restlessness, muscle stiffness, tremor, or abnormal movements—tell your prescriber quickly. Don’t wait it out.
Go to urgent/emergency care for fever + rigidity + confusion, or if you feel faint with chest palpitations.
Stand up slowly—dizziness and blood pressure drops can happen, especially early on.
Avoid alcohol and other sedatives unless your prescriber explicitly okays it—sedation and falls can stack.
If you notice sore throat/fever that doesn’t quit, unusual bruising, or infections, you may need a blood count check.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: The most psychiatry-relevant side effects are movement symptoms (EPS), sedation, dizziness/low blood pressure, and longer-term risk of tardive dyskinesia. Perphenazine can also affect prolactin and, like many antipsychotics, can impact weight and metabolism in some people.
plain_language_list: Restlessness (akathisia) — that “I can’t sit still” feeling
Muscle spasms or abnormal postures (acute dystonia)
Dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, trouble urinating (anticholinergic effects can happen, usually less than some other phenothiazines)
Sexual side effects or hormonal effects from prolactin changes (irregular periods, breast changes, libido changes)

common.patient_note: This is the signature risk zone for perphenazine. Watch for restlessness (akathisia), stiffness, tremor, slowed movement, or jaw/neck muscle tightness. These can show up early and can get worse with dose increases.
Some people feel calmer but sleepy or slowed down—especially early in treatment. If you’re too sedated to function, that’s a dosing/timing problem worth fixing, not a life sentence.
Feeling lightheaded when standing can happen, especially during titration. This matters because it increases fall risk—especially in older adults.

common.symptom: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurry vision, urinary retention)
common.patient_note: Perphenazine has relatively lower anticholinergic potency than some other phenothiazines, but these symptoms can still occur—especially if combined with other anticholinergic meds.
Possible menstrual changes, breast tenderness/enlargement, galactorrhea, libido changes, erectile/ejaculatory issues. If symptoms show up, prolactin can be checked and the plan can be adjusted.

serious: Tardive dyskinesia: Involuntary movements (face, tongue, jaw, limbs) that can become permanent
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): Fever, severe rigidity, confusion, unstable blood pressure/heart rate — MEDICAL EMERGENCY
Serious arrhythmias: Palpitations, fainting, sudden collapse — EMERGENCY
Severe blood dyscrasias (eg, agranulocytosis): Infections, fever, sore throat — urgent evaluation needed
Jaundice or liver injury: Yellow skin/eyes, dark urine, severe fatigue
Seizures: Especially in people with seizure history or other risk factors
Aspiration pneumonia risk: Swallowing problems, choking episodes, cough/fever—especially in older adults

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions

items.with: Alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, sedating sleep meds, sedating antihistamines
items.risk: Additive CNS depression: more sedation, impaired coordination, falls, and in severe cases breathing suppression (especially when multiple sedatives are combined).
items.action: Avoid mixing when possible. If combination is clinically necessary, use lowest effective doses and monitor closely—especially early on.

items.risk: Higher risk of dangerous rhythm problems when multiple QT-risk agents are combined, especially with electrolyte abnormalities.
items.action: Review the full med list for QT risk. Correct low potassium/magnesium and consider ECG monitoring when risk is elevated.

items.risk: Higher perphenazine exposure can increase EPS, sedation, and other adverse effects.
items.action: Use caution. Consider lower dosing and closer monitoring if CYP2D6 inhibition or poor metabolizer risk is present.

items.risk: Additive blood pressure lowering may worsen dizziness and falls.
items.action: Monitor orthostatic vitals and adjust therapy if symptomatic.

items.risk: More constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion (especially in older adults).
items.action: Minimize anticholinergic stacking and watch bowel/bladder symptoms.

items.with: Dopamine agonists (eg, medications used for Parkinson symptoms)
items.risk: Pharmacologic “tug-of-war”: perphenazine blocks dopamine, which can reduce the effect of dopamine-boosting meds and worsen parkinsonism.
items.action: Use caution and coordinate with neurology/psychiatry when both are needed.

sections.intro: Perphenazine has meaningful interaction risks—especially anything that adds sedation, drops blood pressure, affects heart rhythm, or changes CYP2D6 metabolism.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If perphenazine is being stopped (and it’s not an emergency safety situation), a gradual taper is usually the move—especially in chronic psychotic disorders. The goal is to reduce withdrawal symptoms and catch early relapse signs before they become a full crisis.
key_points: In chronic schizophrenia, switching antipsychotics is often preferred over just stopping, especially if symptoms are ongoing or relapse risk is high.
If stopping is patient-driven and not due to a serious adverse reaction, taper over weeks to months when feasible to reduce withdrawal and rebound symptoms.
Possible withdrawal/rebound symptoms: agitation, anxiety, sweating, insomnia, GI symptoms, tremor, restlessness, dizziness/vertigo, dyskinesias, and return/worsening of psychosis.

Switching strategies vary: cross-titration (slowly down on one while slowly up on the other) is common; in high-relapse-risk patients, overlap may be used until the new medication is clearly therapeutic, then taper the original over 1 to 2 weeks (or longer when needed).
If stopping is due to severe adverse effects (eg, NMS, severe dyscrasia, serious arrhythmia), the plan changes—safety first.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Perphenazine dosing for schizophrenia is usually divided across the day. Many people do best when the dose is increased slowly and kept at the lowest effective maintenance dose to reduce EPS and other side effects. First-episode psychosis often requires lower starting doses because sensitivity to adverse effects tends to be higher.

adult.schizophrenia_initial: 8 to 16 mg/day PO in 2 to 3 divided doses
adult.first_episode_lower_start: If first-episode psychosis or highly sensitive to side effects: consider 4 to 8 mg/day PO in divided doses
adult.schizophrenia_titration: May increase in 8 mg/day increments every 4 to 7 days based on response and tolerability; monitor closely for akathisia, anticholinergic effects, orthostasis, parkinsonism, and sedation during titration
adult.schizophrenia_maintenance: Usual maintenance range: 8 to 32 mg/day PO in 2 to 3 divided doses; use the lowest effective maintenance dose
adult.schizophrenia_max: 64 mg/day PO (specialist-level decision; higher dose increases risk of EPS, sedation, and other adverse effects)
adult.older_adult: Refer to adult dosing, but start in the lower end of the range, titrate slowly, and monitor carefully; avoid for behavioral problems of dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic options fail and there is risk of harm
adult.renal: No manufacturer-provided adjustment; use with caution and monitor renal function clinically
adult.hepatic: Should not be used if you have liver damage; liver function is checked during use, and it is stopped if problems appear

sections.simple_explanation: Think of dosing in two phases: (1) finding a dose that controls symptoms without causing unbearable side effects, then (2) staying on the lowest effective maintenance dose. With perphenazine, side effects—especially movement symptoms—often set the ceiling.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Perphenazine can be used in special situations, but the risk-benefit decision has to be individualized—especially in pregnancy, postpartum, and older adults. For psychiatric disorders, specialist guidance is strongly recommended.
sections.pregnancy: Class-level data for first-generation antipsychotics do not show a clear large increase in major congenital malformations, but individual-agent data are limited. Antipsychotic use in the third trimester can increase the risk of newborn EPS and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, abnormal tone, tremor, sleepiness, feeding problems, respiratory distress). Treatment decisions should use shared decision-making: relapse prevention matters, and stopping an effective medication can be risky. Use the lowest effective dose of a single agent when possible and avoid polytherapy unless clearly needed.
sections.lactation: Perphenazine is present in breast milk. Limited data suggest a low relative infant dose in one reported case, and no adverse events were observed in that infant; however, infants exposed to antipsychotics via milk can develop sedation, irritability, poor feeding, or motor abnormalities. If breastfeeding while taking perphenazine, monitor the infant closely—especially if premature, low birth weight, or if other sedating meds are also involved.
sections.geriatrics: High-risk medication in older adults. Antipsychotics are potentially inappropriate for behavioral symptoms of dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic approaches failed and there is risk of harm. Boxed warning: increased mortality in dementia-related psychosis. Older adults are also more vulnerable to orthostatic hypotension, falls, sedation, aspiration, hyponatremia/SIADH, and movement side effects—start low, titrate slow, and reassess often.
sections.hepatic: Contraindicated in liver damage. Monitor hepatic function during therapy and discontinue if clinically significant abnormalities occur.
sections.renal: Use with caution. Monitor renal function clinically; discontinue if concerning abnormalities occur.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mental status and function: symptom change, agitation, suicidality, and overall functioning at every visit
Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS): assess every visit; reassess around 4 weeks after initiation and after dose changes; use a formal rating scale at least annually (or every 6 months if high risk)
Tardive dyskinesia: watch at every visit and perform formalized screening at least annually (or more often if high risk)
Vital signs and orthostatics: especially during initiation/titration and in older adults; monitor fall risk as clinically indicated
Weight/BMI: every visit for the first 6 months, then at least quarterly; consider waist circumference at baseline and annually
Metabolic labs: fasting glucose/HbA1c and lipid panel about 4 months after initiation and then at least annually (more often if abnormal)
Electrolytes and sodium: especially in older adults (SIADH/hyponatremia risk) and when clinically indicated
CBC: as clinically indicated; monitor more closely if prior low WBC or history of drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia; discontinue if severe dyscrasia develops
Liver function tests: as clinically indicated; discontinue if abnormalities occur; be alert for jaundice symptoms
Cardiac risk: consider ECG and electrolyte review when baseline risk is elevated or when combining with QT-risk meds
Adherence and safety behaviors: check at every visit; review sedation, driving safety, and substance use

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Perphenazine is available as an oral tablet in multiple strengths, allowing gradual titration and easier dose adjustments.
items: Oral tablets: 2 mg, 4 mg, 8 mg, 16 mg (generic available)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Perphenazine works mainly by blocking dopamine D2 receptors in brain pathways involved in psychosis. Turning down dopamine signaling in these circuits can reduce hallucinations, delusions, and severe thought disorganization. That same dopamine blockade in movement pathways is also why it can cause EPS and raise tardive dyskinesia risk over time.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Perphenazine is a first-generation antipsychotic option for schizophrenia. Many clinicians prefer second-generation antipsychotics first because they may cause fewer movement side effects for some patients, but perphenazine can still be a valid choice depending on prior response, side effect profile, access, and patient preference. When it’s used, the key is careful titration, proactive monitoring for movement side effects, and sticking with the lowest effective maintenance dose.

faqs.q: What is perphenazine used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: In psychiatry, perphenazine is mainly used to treat schizophrenia—especially symptoms like hallucinations, delusions, paranoia, and severe thought disorganization. It may also be used in select cases for severe psychosis-related agitation, typically with specialist guidance.

faqs.q: How long does perphenazine take to work?
faqs.a: Some early improvement can show up within 1 to 2 weeks (often reduced agitation or reduced intensity of symptoms). Bigger changes usually build over 4 to 6 weeks of consistent treatment.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects to watch for?
faqs.a: The biggest ones are movement side effects (EPS) like restlessness (akathisia), stiffness, tremor and slowed movement. Sleepiness, dizziness (especially when standing up), and dry mouth or constipation can also happen. Over the long term, tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements, often of the face or mouth, that can last) is a serious risk.

faqs.q: What is EPS and why is it such a big deal with perphenazine?
faqs.a: EPS (extrapyramidal symptoms) means movement side effects caused by blocking dopamine in the brain areas that control movement. With perphenazine, EPS can include akathisia (can’t sit still), parkinsonism (stiffness, tremor) and dystonia (painful muscle spasms). These can be distressing and can get in the way of treatment if they aren't dealt with early.

faqs.q: Can perphenazine cause tardive dyskinesia (lasting involuntary movements)?
faqs.a: Yes. Tardive dyskinesia (TD) is a risk with typical antipsychotics, especially with higher doses and longer duration. TD can be irreversible, which is why ongoing monitoring and using the lowest effective dose matters.

faqs.q: Is perphenazine safe for dementia-related agitation or psychosis?
faqs.a: This is a major caution area. Antipsychotics carry a boxed warning: older adults with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death compared with placebo. Perphenazine is not approved for dementia-related psychosis. If an antipsychotic is used at all in that setting, it’s generally reserved for cases where non-drug strategies failed and there’s risk of harm.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking perphenazine?
faqs.a: It’s strongly discouraged. Alcohol can stack sedation, impair coordination, and increase fall risk. Combining multiple sedating substances can also increase risk of serious complications. If alcohol use is part of your life, bring it up early so the plan is realistic and safe.

faqs.q: How do you stop perphenazine safely?
faqs.a: Unless there’s a serious safety reason to stop immediately, perphenazine is usually tapered gradually—especially in chronic psychotic disorders. A slower reduction helps reduce withdrawal symptoms (agitation, insomnia, sweating, GI upset, tremor) and helps catch early relapse signs before they escalate.

No. Antipsychotics are generally not used for catatonia. In people with catatonia, they may worsen psychosis and raise the risk of a rare emergency with very high fever and rigid muscles (neuroleptic malignant syndrome, NMS). Catatonia needs its own targeted treatment.

faqs.q: Does perphenazine affect pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Decisions in pregnancy and breastfeeding are individualized. Class-level data for first-generation antipsychotics don’t show a clear large increase in major congenital malformations, but newborn EPS/withdrawal symptoms are a concern with third-trimester exposure. Perphenazine can pass into breast milk; limited data suggest low infant exposure in one case, but infants should be monitored for sedation, feeding issues, and motor changes.
